# What's special about time {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Why order matters

In a normal table you can shuffle the rows without losing anything. In a time series you cannot: the order carries information. It gives you three things:

- **Trend** — long-run direction
- **Seasonality** — repeating cycles (daily, weekly, annual)
- **Autocorrelation** — today resembles yesterday

It also creates practical problems: gaps, irregular sampling, time zones, and the choice of **resolution** — how finely you slice time before plotting.

## First, make the dates real dates {.smaller}

A column of dates read from a CSV is text, not time. Convert it with `pd.to_datetime`:

```{python}
#| echo: true
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.DataFrame({"when": ["2024-01-05", "2024-02-05", "2024-03-05"],
                    "ppm":  [421.0, 422.4, 423.1]})
print("before:", raw["when"].dtype)
raw["when"] = pd.to_datetime(raw["when"])
print("after: ", raw["when"].dtype)
```

Until you convert, pandas treats the values as strings. That means they sort alphabetically, you cannot subtract them, and `resample` and `rolling` are unavailable.

::: {.gw-box}
`"03/04/2024"` is 3 April in most of the world and 4 March in the US. Pandas has to guess unless you tell it: pass `format="%d/%m/%Y"`, or `dayfirst=True`. Add `errors="coerce"` to turn unparseable values into `NaT` instead of stopping with an error.
:::

## What a DatetimeIndex gives you {.smaller}

Once the dates are the **index**, pandas understands the calendar:

```{python}
#| echo: true
d = pd.Series(range(90), index=pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=90, freq="D"))

print(d.loc["2024-02"].head(2))          # slice a whole month by name
print(d.resample("MS").mean().round(1))  # month-start averages
print(d.index.day_name()[:3].tolist())   # calendar parts
```

- **Slicing by string** — `d.loc["2024-02"]` or `d.loc["2024-02":"2024-03"]`, no masks needed
- **`resample`** — change the resolution: `"D"` day, `"W"` week, `"MS"` month-start, `"YS"` year-start
- **`.index` accessors** — `.year`, `.month`, `.dayofweek`, `.day_name()` for grouping by calendar parts
- **Time-aware `rolling`** — `d.rolling("30D")` uses a 30-*day* window, which is not the same as `d.rolling(30)` when rows are unevenly spaced

## Resolution changes what you see

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.api as sm
co2 = sm.datasets.co2.load_pandas().data.dropna()
weekly = co2["co2"]
monthly = weekly.resample("MS").mean().dropna()
yearly = weekly.resample("YS").mean()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6), sharey=True)
weekly.loc["1990":"1995"].plot(ax=axes[0], color="#2E6E8E")
axes[0].set_title("Weekly, 1990–95: the seasonal sawtooth dominates")
yearly.plot(ax=axes[1], color="#2E6E8E")
axes[1].set_title("Yearly means: only the trend survives")
for a in axes: a.set_ylabel("CO₂ (ppm)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Neither chart is wrong. **Resolution is a choice you make, so choose it deliberately and state it on the chart.**

## Autocorrelation, made visible {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 2.05))
plot_acf(monthly, lags=36, ax=axes[0], title="")
axes[0].set_title("Raw series: trend dominates — everything correlates", fontsize=9.5)
plot_acf(monthly.diff().dropna(), lags=36, ax=axes[1], title="")
axes[1].set_title("After differencing: a clean spike at lag 12", fontsize=9.5)
for a in axes: a.set_xlabel("lag (months)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The **ACF** plots the correlation of the series with itself at each lag.

**Left** — the raw series. Correlation stays high at every lag because the whole series is rising, so the trend hides everything else.

**Right** — the same series after **differencing**, which is what `.diff()` does: each value is replaced by the change since the previous month. The trend drops out, and the month-to-month movement that remains shows **seasonality** as a spike at lag 12, repeating at 24 and 36.

::: {.gw-box}
**Differencing, concretely.** `s.diff()` turns `421.0, 422.4, 423.1` into `1.4, 0.7` — changes instead of levels. One `.diff()` removes a straight-line trend. `s.diff(12)` subtracts the value from twelve months earlier, which removes an annual cycle instead.
:::

# Trend & seasonality {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Smoothing reveals trend

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
monthly = co2["co2"].resample("MS").mean().dropna()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.8))
monthly.plot(ax=ax, alpha=0.35, label="monthly")
monthly.rolling(12).mean().plot(ax=ax, linewidth=2, label="12-month rolling mean")
ax.set_ylabel("CO₂ (ppm)"); ax.legend()
ax.set_title("A 12-month window averages out exactly one seasonal cycle")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Window length is a choice. Matching the window to the **seasonal period** is a sensible default. The next slide shows what different windows do to the same series.

## What the window length does {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
seg4 = monthly.loc["1980":"1998"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.8, 2.9))
seg4.plot(ax=axes[0], color="#bbbbbb", lw=0.9, label="monthly")
for w, c in [(3, "#d9534f"), (12, "#2E6E8E"), (60, "#6aa84f")]:
    seg4.rolling(w).mean().plot(ax=axes[0], lw=1.8, color=c, label=f"{w}-month")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=6.5); axes[0].set_ylabel("CO₂ (ppm)")
axes[0].set_title("Rolling mean: 3 keeps the season, 12 removes it, 60 flattens", fontsize=9)

seg4.rolling(12).std().plot(ax=axes[1], color="#b07aa1", lw=1.8)
axes[1].set_ylabel("ppm"); axes[1].set_xlabel("")
axes[1].set_title("Rolling std: the *amplitude* of the seasonal swing", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

- **3 months** — shorter than the cycle, so the sawtooth survives: you are smoothing noise, not seasonality
- **12 months** — exactly one cycle, so seasonality cancels and trend remains
- **60 months** — erases real turning points along with the noise

The window changes what the chart says, so report it. You can also roll statistics other than the mean: the right panel rolls the **standard deviation**, which shows how the size of the seasonal swing changes over time.

## Decomposition: splitting the series into three parts {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose
res = seasonal_decompose(monthly, period=12)
fig = res.plot()
fig.set_size_inches(8.3, 4.2)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The series is split into trend, seasonal, and residual. The **residual panel is the diagnostic**: if a pattern is still visible there, the decomposition has missed something. The next slide uses that to choose between two models.

## Additive or multiplicative? Check the residuals {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
rng4 = np.random.default_rng(11)
n4 = 132
idx = pd.date_range("2008-01-01", periods=n4, freq="MS")
level = np.linspace(100, 320, n4)
# Swing AND noise both scale with the level — the multiplicative signature.
series = pd.Series(level * (1 + 0.16 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * np.arange(n4) / 12))
                   * (1 + rng4.normal(0, 0.012, n4)), index=idx)

add = seasonal_decompose(series, period=12, model="additive")
mul = seasonal_decompose(series, period=12, model="multiplicative")

# NB: plot through matplotlib, not Series.plot() — pandas installs its own date
# converter, which silently ignores the mdates locator and blanks the labels.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.2, 2.7))
axes[0].plot(series.index, series.values, color="#2E6E8E", lw=1.3)
axes[0].set_title("Swing grows with the level", fontsize=9)
axes[1].plot(add.resid.index, add.resid.values, color="#d9534f", lw=1.0)
axes[1].axhline(0, color="#999999", lw=0.7)
axes[1].set_title("Additive residual: big at both ends", fontsize=9)
axes[2].plot(mul.resid.index, mul.resid.values, color="#6aa84f", lw=1.0)
axes[2].axhline(1, color="#999999", lw=0.7)
axes[2].set_title("Multiplicative residual: no pattern", fontsize=9)
for a in axes:
    a.set_xlabel("")
    a.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator(3))
    a.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y"))
    a.tick_params(labelsize=7)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Additive** assumes a seasonal swing of constant size (`trend + seasonal + resid`). **Multiplicative** assumes it scales with the level (`trend × seasonal × resid`) — the usual case for anything growing, like sales or traffic.

Fitting additive here estimates **one averaged swing**, which is too big early and too small late. So the residual is large at both ends and near zero in the middle — the single point where the average happens to fit.

::: {.gw-box}
To choose between them, fit one and **look at the residual panel**. A pattern left in the residuals means the other model fits better. CO₂ is additive; most business series are multiplicative.
:::

# Uncertainty {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Show the uncertainty, not just the line

A time series carries uncertainty from three sources: measurement error, the smoothing choices you made, and, for forecasts, the model itself. A plain line shows none of them.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
roll = monthly.rolling(12)
mean, std = roll.mean(), roll.std()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.2))
mean.plot(ax=ax, label="12-mo mean", color="#2E6E8E")
ax.fill_between(mean.index, mean - 2*std, mean + 2*std, alpha=0.2, color="#2E6E8E", label="±2σ band")
ax.set_ylabel("CO₂ (ppm)"); ax.legend()
ax.set_title("The band shows how far values typically sit from the smooth line")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Bands, error bars, and intervals return in Week 13, where the same methods are used to show **model** uncertainty.

# Showing time with animation {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Animation uses frames instead of an axis {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
import plotly.express as px
gap = px.data.gapminder()
figa = px.scatter(gap, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", size="pop", color="continent",
                  hover_name="country", animation_frame="year", log_x=True,
                  size_max=42, range_y=[25, 90], height=350, width=1080,
                  labels={"gdpPercap": "GDP per capita", "lifeExp": "life expectancy"})
figa.update_layout(margin=dict(l=4, r=4, t=6, b=0), legend=dict(font=dict(size=10)))
figa
```

Press play. Every other chart today puts time on an **axis**. This one uses animation frames for time instead, which leaves both axes free for other variables — five variables are shown here at once.

## What animation gains and loses {.smaller}

**What it gains** — the change from 1952 to 2007 is easy to follow, and motion draws attention automatically (preattentive attributes, Week 2), so viewers notice whatever moves most.

**What it loses** — **persistence**. A static chart lets the reader compare any two points whenever they like. An animation shows one frame at a time, so comparing two years means remembering the earlier one or replaying it.

::: {.gw-box}
A useful rule: animate when the goal is to **engage**, and use small multiples or an overlay when the goal is to **compare**. A question such as "how much did this change between 1980 and 2000" is easier to answer from a static chart.
:::

# Honesty on the time axis {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Truncated axes

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
seg = monthly.loc["1984":"1989"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
seg.plot(ax=axes[0], color="#d9534f")
axes[0].set_ylim(seg.min()-0.5, seg.max()+0.5)
axes[0].set_title("Truncated axis: the rise looks dramatic")
seg.plot(ax=axes[1], color="#2E6E8E")
axes[1].set_ylim(0, seg.max()*1.1)
axes[1].set_title("Zero baseline: steady ~1.5 ppm/yr rise")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Both panels show the same data. Truncating the axis is not always wrong, since small changes can matter. But the truncation should be **visible and stated** rather than silent.

## Aspect ratio changes the perceived slope {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
seg5 = yearly.loc["1965":"2000"]
yrs = seg5.index.year          # integers, so a tick locator actually applies
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 2.8), sharey=True,
                         gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 2.2, 5]})
for a, t in zip(axes, ["tall & narrow:\n'runaway'", "banked near 45°:\nreadable",
                       "wide & flat:\n'nothing happening'"]):
    a.plot(yrs, seg5.values, color="#2E6E8E", lw=1.8)
    a.set_title(t, fontsize=8.5); a.set_xlabel("")
    a.xaxis.set_major_locator(plt.MaxNLocator(3, integer=True))
    a.tick_params(labelsize=6.5)
axes[0].set_ylabel("CO₂ (ppm)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

All three panels show the same data over the same y-range. **Only the width changed**, and that alone changes how fast the rise appears.

::: {.gw-box}
Cleveland's **banking to 45°**: people judge slopes most accurately when the average line segment is close to 45°. Moving far from that makes the figure's shape part of the argument.
:::

## The honesty checklist for temporal charts {.smaller}

- Y-axis: zero-based, or truncation **flagged**
- Resolution: stated, chosen for the question
- Smoothing: window disclosed
- Aspect ratio: not stretched to exaggerate the slope
- Dual axes: avoid them; they can make unrelated series look related

::: {.gw-box}
Week 14 covers ethics in full. Most everyday misleading charts involve the time axis.
:::
